# Words and Numbers {#chp:strings}

Text is where most of the everyday fiddling happens: matching a pattern and
rewriting it, deciding whether a string is empty, stitching words into a
sentence, or turning a label into something safe to use as an HTML ID. The
recipes here cover those jobs, plus spelling out numbers for reports.

## Filter and transform in one step {#sec:grep-sub}

You often want the elements that match a pattern, and you want them rewritten
too. `grep_sub()` combines `grep(..., value = TRUE)` and `gsub()` into one call:

```{r}
grep_sub('(\\w+)@(\\w+)', '\\2/\\1', c('alice@corp', 'bob@org', 'not-an-email'))
```

The emails that did not match are dropped, and the ones that did come back
rewritten.

## Spot blank strings {#sec:is-blank}

An empty string is not `NA`, and a string of spaces is not empty, yet both look
blank on screen. `is_blank()` catches empty strings and strings made only of
whitespace:

```{r}
is_blank(c("", "   ", "\t\n", "hello"))
```

## Join words into a sentence {#sec:join-words}

Turning a vector into a readable list is a small task that everyone rewrites
from scratch. `join_words()` adds the conjunction, and the Oxford comma, for
you:

```{r}
join_words(c("apples", "oranges", "pears"))
join_words(c("R", "Python", "Julia"), and = "or ")
join_words(c("one", "two", "three"), before = "'", after = "'")
```

## Make safe IDs from any text {#sec:alnum-id}

Headings and labels often end up as HTML IDs, and spaces, punctuation, or tags
in them are trouble. `alnum_id()` replaces non-alphanumeric characters with
dashes and strips HTML tags on the way:

```{r}
alnum_id(c("Hello world 123!", "a  &b*^c"))
alnum_id("<h1>Section <em>1.2</em></h1>")
```

## Spell out numbers {#sec:n2w}

In a report, "three hundred five" often reads better than "305", and it is
tedious to type by hand. `n2w()` (the alias `numbers_to_words()` is also
available) does it for you. It handles capitalization, the word "and", and
negative numbers:

```{r}
n2w(c(0, 1, 13, 42, 100, 1001), cap = TRUE)
n2w(1e6 + 234567, and = TRUE)
n2w(-987654321)
```

## Wrap long text into single strings {#sec:str-wrap}

`strwrap()` returns a flat vector of lines, so the output no longer lines up
with the input. `str_wrap()` takes the same arguments but returns one string per
input element, with the lines joined by `\n`:

```{r}
x = c('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.', 'Short one.')
str_wrap(x, 20)
cat(str_wrap(x, 20), sep = '\n\n')
```

Two strings in, two strings out, so the result still fits in a data frame
column.

## Split text into lines safely {#sec:split-lines}

`strsplit(x, '\n')` has two surprises: an empty string becomes
`character(0)`, and a trailing newline is silently dropped. `split_lines()`
splits on `\n` and keeps both:

```{r}
strsplit(c('', 'a\nb\n'), '\n')
split_lines(c('', 'a\nb\n'))
```

The result is always one flat vector, so `length()` counts lines the way an
editor would.

## Check for non-ASCII characters {#sec:is-ascii}

Before writing text to a file or package that insists on ASCII, find out which
elements will cause trouble. `is_ascii()` tells you element by element:

```{r}
is_ascii(c('abc', 'café', '你好'))
```

## Convert text to the native encoding {#sec:native-encode}

On a system whose native encoding is not UTF-8, writing UTF-8 strings may
garble them. `native_encode()` converts to the native encoding only if no
information is lost; otherwise it returns the input unchanged, with a warning:

```{r}
native_encode('café')
```

On UTF-8 platforms the conversion is skipped, so this is a no-op there.

## Fingerprint any R object {#sec:md5}

`tools::md5sum()` only works on files. `md5()` serializes any R objects and
returns their checksums, which is handy for cache keys or for checking whether
a result changed. Named arguments give named results:

```{r}
md5(1:10, mtcars)
md5(a = 'x', b = 'y')
```

## Label rows by their combination of values {#sec:radix-id}

To flag duplicates across several columns, pasting them into one string is slow
on big data. `radix_id()` encodes each row as a single number instead, with
`NA` as its own category. Equal combinations get equal codes:

```{r}
g = c('a', 'b', 'a', 'b', NA)
h = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 1)
id = radix_id(g, h)
id
!duplicated(id)
```

The codes themselves are only good for equality checks, not for ordering or
arithmetic.

## Number the groups {#sec:radix-group}

When you need group numbers you can actually use, `radix_group()` returns
integers `1:k` in order of first appearance:

```{r}
radix_group(g, h)
```

Rows 1 and 3 share group 1, and the `NA` row gets its own group.

## Generate reproducible random numbers {#sec:rand-unit}

`rand_unit()` is a tiny linear congruential generator that returns numbers in
`[0, 1)`. Unlike `runif()`, it does not touch R's `.Random.seed`, and the same
seed gives the same numbers on any machine:

```{r}
rand_unit(3, seed = 1)
rand_unit(3, seed = 1)
```

Without `seed`, a call continues from where the previous call stopped.

## Force a dot as the decimal separator {#sec:decimal-dot}

In some locales, or after `options(OutDec = ',')`, converting a number to
character gives `1,5`. That breaks anything that expects machine-readable
numbers, such as JSON or code. `decimal_dot()` evaluates an expression with the
dot restored:

```{r}
op = options(OutDec = ',')
paste(1.5)
decimal_dot(paste(1.5))
options(op)
```
